options: A hidden .git folder in the current directory, which stores the project's entire Git history
A new GitHub repository automatically
A backup copy of the folder on another drive
A .gitconfig file with your identity settings
questions.explain: git init turns a plain folder into a Git repository by creating the .git folder where all history is stored.

questions.q: What are the three states a tracked file moves through in Git?
options: Draft, Review, Published
Local, Remote, Archived
Working directory, staging area, repository
Open, Staged, Closed
questions.explain: A file is edited in the working directory, marked with git add into the staging area, then permanently recorded via git commit into the repository.

questions.q: Why would you stage only one of three unrelated changed files with `git add`, instead of `git add .` for all three?
options: git add . is not a valid command
So the commit stays deliberate — each commit can represent one coherent change instead of "whatever happened to be unsaved at the time"
Staging specific files is required for Git to work at all
It has no practical difference and is purely a style preference
questions.explain: Selective staging lets you build commits that each represent one logical change, which makes history far more useful later.

questions.q: What makes a commit message like "fix off-by-one error in totals when the last row is empty" better than "fix bug"?
options: It's longer, and Git requires a minimum message length
It tells a future reader what actually changed and why, rather than nothing useful at all
There's no real difference — Git displays both identically
Short messages are not allowed by git commit
questions.explain: A specific commit message is what makes git log useful months later; "fix bug" gives no information about what was fixed.

options: A list of files currently staged
The commit history, newest first, with each commit's hash, author, date, and message
A list of all branches in the repository
The contents of the .gitignore file
questions.explain: git log is the tracked history itself — every commit, in order, with its identifying details.
